lesson.title: Project clinic: turn a topic into a falsifiable research question
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: “Use a GPU for databases” is a topic. A research question names a mechanism, a comparison, a workload and a possible failure.
goals: Write a bounded research claim with a falsification condition.
Connect a proposed mechanism to an observed bottleneck.
Prepare concrete evidence and decisions for an instructor consultation.

sections.title: How to use this supplemental session
sections.html: This is an original supplemental study session aligned to the user-provided syllabus. It is not an Edinburgh lecture or a verified Canvas assignment. The Canvas reading list and instructor-specific assessment instructions were not accessible. Suggested activities, timings, templates and checks below are practice guidance, not official requirements.

sections.title: The research-question contract
sections.html:
Write one sentence with five parts: mechanism, baseline, workload/conditions, metric and constraint. Example: “For public 768-dimensional embeddings at small query batches, does a fixed-budget graph-search policy lower p95 latency relative to a tuned fixed policy while preserving recall@10 ≥0.95?” This is a suggested research question, not a claim that the method will work or be novel.

State the null possibility: the policy may add overhead, lose recall on difficult queries or fail to generalize. Name the smallest experiment that could expose that failure. A good question remains informative when the result is negative.

Distinguish reproduction (re-running a published claim under declared conditions), replication/generalization (testing the claim with changed data or implementation), and extension (introducing a new mechanism). Define your usage because communities sometimes use these words differently. Novelty requires a literature check; it is not established by a new repository.

Key takeaway

A narrow question with a credible baseline is stronger than a broad system with no testable claim.

sections.title: Use a causal chain to justify the mechanism
sections.html:
Start from a measured symptom and trace why it happens. Example: low GPU utilization → tiny query batches → insufficient parallel work per launch → batch accumulation might improve throughput → waiting to form a batch might increase latency. That last arrow creates a trade-off worth testing.

For every arrow, list an observable: batch-size distribution, queue delay, device execution time and end-to-end latency. If only final QPS is measured, a faster result cannot explain the cause. If the true bottleneck is host-side preprocessing, optimizing a search kernel may have little effect.

Construct a minimal prototype to test the critical arrow. A two-day feasibility check that disproves an assumption can save the rest of the project. Time boxes here are illustrative planning choices, not syllabus deadlines.

Exercise: “LLMs improve query optimization.” Rewrite it as a research question.

Worked answer. One possible version: “On a held-out set of multi-table query templates, can an LLM-based selector choose among the same ten legal plans faster end-to-end than a native optimizer, after including selection latency and with no increase in timeout count?” It specifies the decision, baseline, domain, costs and risk. A simpler non-LLM ranker is also an important comparator.

sections.title: Build a literature-and-evidence matrix
sections.html:
For each close paper, record: exact title/venue/year; problem; key assumption; mechanism; strongest baseline; dataset; metric; artifact; reported limitation; and the difference from your proposal. Add a short “what would I need to reproduce this?” note.

Keep publication status separate. An arXiv manuscript can correspond to an accepted paper when a primary record confirms it; a preprint without such evidence must remain labeled a preprint. Do not infer acceptance from a repository badge or a third-party summary. For assigned reading, use the actual instructor list when it becomes available; the frontier bibliography here is supplemental.

Read the benchmark protocol as carefully as the abstract. Learned-optimizer evaluation and ANN methodology provide examples of how data splits and recall thresholds can change the interpretation of a result.

Primary sources: Is Your Learned Query Optimizer Behaving As You Expect? A Machine Learning Perspective; NVIDIA cuVS: Benchmarking methodologies.

sections.title: Worked example: a one-page research charter
sections.html:
Original example charter.

  • Question: When does microbatching improve end-to-end ANN throughput under a p95 latency budget?
  • Motivation: Batch-1 device utilization is low in a preliminary trace; this observation must first be measured.
  • Mechanism: Accumulate arrivals for a bounded waiting window before a search call.
  • Baselines: Immediate dispatch and a tuned fixed-size batching policy, using identical index/search parameters.
  • Independent variables: Arrival rate, waiting-window cap and query difficulty. Hold dataset, GPU and recall target fixed.
  • Evidence: Arrival-to-response p50/p95/p99, queue time, execution time, QPS, achieved recall and dropped/failed queries.
  • Falsification: Throughput gains disappear at matched p95, or difficult-query recall violates the target.
  • Deliverable: A reproducible plot and explanation of the useful operating range, including where batching loses.

Check that the load generator can produce the intended arrival process and is not itself the bottleneck. Under overload, a closed-loop client can hide queue growth; state whether load is open- or closed-loop.

sections.title: Prepare an instructor consultation that can change the project
sections.html:
The syllabus mentions supervised research and instructor consultations. Exact appointments, required documents and approval rules have not been verified. The following agenda is a useful preparation template.

  1. Show the one-sentence question and a diagram of the measured bottleneck.
  2. Bring the closest prior paper and the precise proposed difference.
  3. Show one preliminary result or a minimal failure trace, with configuration and uncertainty.
  4. List two concrete decisions, such as “Is this baseline appropriate?” and “Should the scope prioritize filtered recall or update freshness?”
  5. Record the instructor’s actual answer, resulting change, owner and next evidence needed. Do not turn an informal suggestion into an invented grading rule.
Exercise: a project needs four GPUs but only one is available. What is a rigorous rescope?

Worked answer. Study a single-device mechanism or a controlled model of communication overhead, and narrow the claim accordingly. Do not label single-node emulation a reproduction of a four-GPU scaling result. Record the hardware limitation and ask whether the revised question fits the course’s actual expectations.

Key takeaway

Bring a decision and the evidence needed to make it, rather than a list of activities.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest project starting point?
options: Build the fastest possible database.
Use every available GPU.
Implement a paper without reading its evaluation.
Test a specific mechanism against a fair baseline under a stated workload and constraint.
quiz.explanation: A testable claim connects scope, mechanism and evidence; implementation size alone does not make a research contribution.

questions.question: Which element makes a research hypothesis falsifiable?
options: A condition under which evidence would contradict it.
A promise to use the newest model.
A sufficiently ambitious title.
A large number of implementation files.
questions.explanation: A falsifiable hypothesis specifies an observable failure condition, not just the desired result.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What should an instructor consultation ideally bring?
options: Invented grading criteria.
Only a broad topic name.
Concrete evidence, a scoped question and decisions that need guidance.
An untested claim of success.
questions.explanation: A consultation is more useful when the instructor can evaluate a choice using actual assumptions and evidence. Required formats remain instructor-specific.

questions.question: A project needs four GPUs but one is available. Which response preserves scientific integrity?
options: Pretend the one GPU is four devices.
Hide the hardware configuration.
State that four-GPU scaling is proven analytically without a model.
Narrow the question to a single-device mechanism and disclose the new scope.
questions.explanation: Rescoping is legitimate when the revised evidence matches the revised claim. Do not claim measurements from unavailable hardware.

questions.question: How should an arXiv paper with no verified venue acceptance be labeled?
options: As assigned course reading.
As a preprint until acceptance/publication is verified from a reliable primary record.
As peer-reviewed whenever code is public.
As a SIGMOD paper if its topic is databases.
questions.explanation: Repository availability and subject area do not establish acceptance or assignment status.

lqo.authors: Claude Lehmann, Pavel Sulimov, Kurt Stockinger
lqo.supports: An end-to-end learned-optimizer evaluation framework; sensitivity to training/test design; PostgreSQL wins in most tested comparisons, depending on split. This is evidence about the evaluated systems and protocol, not impossibility of learned optimization.
